quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what crimp is, how it is defined and what it does to a fabric design.

questions.q: What does the lecture mean by crimp?
options: The number of threads per inch
The waviness a yarn takes as it bends over the crossing threads
questions.explain: Crimp is the waviness of a yarn in the cloth caused by bending over and under the crossing threads; twist, sett and shrinkage are different things.

questions.q: Which expression defines crimp percentage, as in the lecture?
questions.explain: Crimp % = (straightened − cloth) ÷ cloth × 100; the divisor is the cloth length, and the extra yarn length is the numerator.

questions.q: Which of these does the lecture NOT list as something crimp decides?
options: How densely the cloth can be set
How much yarn a design consumes
How thick and extensible the cloth is
questions.explain: Crimp decides yarn consumption, thickness, extensibility and the maximum density of sett; colour has nothing to do with geometry.

questions.q: In a jammed plain weave of equal yarns, warp and weft crimp are both 20.9 %.
questions.explain: The lecture gives 20.9 % in both directions for a jammed plain weave of equal yarns, the limiting case of Peirce's geometry.

questions.q: What crimp does the lecture give for a 2/2 twill?
questions.explain: A 2/2 twill has fewer interlacings per thread, so it needs only 13.1 % crimp against 20.9 % for jammed plain weave.

questions.q: In the lecture's warp rib example, how is the crimp distributed?
options: About 57 % in the warp and none in the weft
57 % in the weft and none in the warp
questions.explain: A warp rib bends the warp sharply around straight weft, so the warp may take 57 % crimp and the weft none.

questions.q: In Peirce's geometry what does the symbol θ stand for?
options: The crimp angle of the yarn
questions.explain: θ is the angle the yarn makes as it bends over the crossing thread; d is diameter, p is spacing and l the modular length.

questions.q: A 'jammed' structure is one in which the threads are spaced so closely that the yarns cannot be set any denser without distortion.
questions.explain: Jamming is the geometric limit of sett: the bending yarn touches both neighbouring crossing threads and no room is left to close the spacing further.

questions.q: Where does the lecture say the full derivation and live calculator for crimp are found?
questions.explain: The lecture repeats Peirce's geometry for the design course and points to Weaving Calculations 15–16 for the derivation and calculator.

questions.q: In the symbols p₂ = 1.732 d₁, what do p₂ and d₁ represent?
options: A thread spacing and a yarn diameter
A crimp percentage and a count
A pick rate and a loom width
questions.explain: p stands for thread spacing and d for yarn diameter; the subscripts distinguish the two thread systems.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Direction of effect: how crimp moves with weave, diameters and spacing in Peirce's geometry.

questions.q: For a jammed plain weave of equal yarns, which relation does the lecture give?
questions.explain: With equal yarns jammed, the spacing is √3 = 1.732 times the diameter; 2.828 applies when the weft is twice the warp diameter.

questions.q: When the weft diameter is twice the warp diameter in a jammed plain weave, the lecture gives…
questions.explain: The lecture states p₂ = 2.828 d₁ (2√2) for the case of weft twice the warp diameter.

questions.q: If the yarn diameter d₁ doubles in a jammed plain weave of equal yarns, the jammed spacing p₂…
questions.explain: p₂ is proportional to d₁ (p₂ = 1.732 d₁), so doubling the diameter doubles the minimum spacing and halves the maximum threads per unit length.

questions.q: Changing from plain weave to 2/2 twill with the same yarns, the crimp…
options: falls, because each thread interlaces half as often
questions.explain: Fewer interlacings per repeat mean less bending; the lecture's figures fall from 20.9 % to 13.1 %.

questions.q: Higher crimp means a design consumes more yarn per metre of cloth.
questions.explain: Yarn length = cloth length × (1 + crimp), so more crimp means more yarn, which matters for costing.

questions.q: Which fabric property increases with crimp, according to the lecture?
questions.explain: Crimped yarns can straighten under load, so a cloth with more crimp stretches more; the lecture lists thickness and extensibility.

questions.q: A design is woven with its weft held almost straight. Where does the crimp go?
questions.explain: If one system is straight the other must do all the bending, as in the warp rib where the warp takes 57 % and the weft none.

questions.q: Because crimp is a ratio of lengths, it has no units and the same value results whether lengths are measured in inches or centimetres.
questions.explain: Crimp = (straightened − cloth) ÷ cloth is dimensionless; the units cancel.

questions.q: A plain cloth is set below its jammed sett. Compared with the jammed value of 20.9 %, its crimp is…
options: lower, since the yarns bend less around wider-spaced threads
questions.explain: 20.9 % is the maximum for a jammed plain weave of equal yarns; wider spacing lets the yarn lie flatter with less crimp.

questions.q: Which quantity is found as 1 ÷ p₂ when p₂ is in centimetres?
options: Threads per cm of the system spaced by p₂
questions.explain: Spacing and thread density are reciprocals: threads per cm = 1 ÷ spacing in cm.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Crimp percentages, yarn consumption and jammed spacings worked from the lecture's constants.

questions.q: A warp thread 20 cm long in the cloth straightens to 22.4 cm. What is its crimp percentage?
A weft thread straightens to 10.5 cm from a cloth length of 10 cm. What is the crimp percentage?
The warp crimp of a design is 9 %. How many metres of warp yarn does each end consume per 100 m of cloth?
questions.explain: Yarn length = cloth length × (1 + crimp) = 100 × 1.09 = 109 m.

questions.q: A warp of 3,000 ends is woven into 500 m of cloth with 8 % warp crimp. How many metres of warp yarn are used in total?
Equal yarns of diameter 0.02 cm are woven into a jammed plain weave. Using p₂ = 1.732 d₁, what is the thread spacing in cm? Give four decimals.
With a spacing p₂ of 0.0346 cm, how many threads per cm can the jammed cloth hold? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: Threads per cm = 1 ÷ 0.0346 = 28.9.

questions.q: In a jammed plain weave the weft diameter is twice the warp diameter d₁ = 0.015 cm. Using p₂ = 2.828 d₁, what is p₂ in cm? Give four decimals.
A cloth in jammed 2/2 twill has 13.1 % crimp. If 50 cm of cloth is cut, how long does a thread from it straighten to? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: Straightened length = 50 × 1.131 = 56.55 ≈ 56.6 cm.

questions.q: A warp rib has 57 % warp crimp and 0 % weft crimp. For 100 m of cloth, how much warp yarn length per end and how much weft length per pick (over 1 m width) are needed?
options: 157 m per end; 1.57 m per pick
157 m per end; 1.00 m per pick
100 m per end; 1.57 m per pick
57 m per end; 1.00 m per pick
questions.explain: Warp: 100 × 1.57 = 157 m; weft with no crimp: exactly the cloth width, 1.00 m per pick.

questions.q: Equal yarns are woven as jammed plain (20.9 %) and as jammed 2/2 twill (13.1 %). Over 1,000 m of cloth, how much more warp yarn per end does the plain weave need?

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Design-office and costing decisions where crimp changes yarn requirement, sett and cloth behaviour.

questions.q: A costing clerk works out warp yarn requirement from cloth length alone, ignoring crimp. What is the result?
options: Yarn requirement is under-estimated and the warp runs short
No effect, crimp is only cosmetic
questions.explain: Each end needs cloth length × (1 + crimp); leaving out crimp of, say, 10 % means 10 % too little warp is bought.

questions.q: Two cloths use the same yarn: one is a plain weave near jamming, the other a 2/2 twill. Which can be set with more threads per inch?
options: Neither can exceed the yarn diameter
questions.explain: Fewer interlacings let the twill's threads lie closer; its lower crimp (13.1 % vs 20.9 %) goes with a denser jammed sett.

questions.q: A buyer wants a plain fabric that stretches more in the warp direction. Which design change helps?
options: Hold the warp straight and crimp the weft
Increase warp crimp by setting the weft coarser or denser
questions.explain: Extensibility comes from crimp straightening under load, so more warp crimp gives more warp stretch.

questions.q: A warp rib design is being costed. The sample shows the weft lying straight. Which yarn should carry the crimp allowance in the costing?
questions.explain: In a warp rib the weft is straight and the warp does the bending, so the warp consumption carries the large allowance.

questions.q: A thicker cloth from the same yarns can be obtained by choosing a weave and sett that give more crimp.
questions.explain: The lecture lists thickness among the things crimp decides: more bending lifts the yarns further from the cloth plane.

questions.q: A weaver tries to beat up a plain cloth of equal yarns beyond p₂ = 1.732 d₁. What happens?
options: The structure is jammed; the picks cannot be forced closer without distorting the yarns
questions.explain: 1.732 d₁ is the jammed spacing; beyond it there is no geometric room for the yarn to bend between neighbours.

questions.q: A mill switches a plain sheeting to a coarser weft while keeping the warp. What happens to warp crimp and warp yarn consumption?
options: Both increase, since the warp must bend round a larger weft
questions.explain: A larger crossing diameter forces the warp to bend more; more crimp means more warp yarn per metre.

questions.q: Which document should a designer consult, according to the lecture, to calculate θ, spacing, cover factor and crimp for an arbitrary pair of yarn diameters?
options: The live calculator in Weaving Calculations 15–16
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly points to the live calculator for any pair of diameters.

questions.q: For a costing, the weft crimp allowance should be applied to the loom width in the reed, not to the finished cloth width.
questions.explain: Weft length per pick = width in the reed × (1 + weft crimp); the finished width is narrower because of contraction, so using it under-estimates weft.

questions.q: A sample is found to have 25 % crimp in both directions in a plain weave of equal yarns. What should the analyst suspect?
options: A measurement error, since 20.9 % is the jammed maximum for this case
That the cloth is a twill
questions.explain: The lecture gives 20.9 % as the jammed limit for plain weave of equal yarns; a higher reading suggests mis-measurement or stretched threads.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder two-step problems and common mistakes in crimp, consumption and Peirce's constants.

questions.q: A student measures a 10 cm cloth length and a 12.09 cm straightened length and reports crimp as 12.09 ÷ 10 = 120.9 %. What is the correct crimp percentage? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: Crimp = (12.09 − 10) ÷ 10 = 0.209 = 20.9 %; the student forgot to subtract 1.

questions.q: A cloth's warp crimp is 20.9 %. A straightened warp thread measures 30.0 cm. What length of cloth did it come from? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: Cloth length = straightened ÷ (1 + crimp) = 30 ÷ 1.209 = 24.8 cm.

questions.q: Warp rib (57 % warp crimp, 0 % weft) and plain weave (20.9 % both) are compared at 2,400 ends and 2,000 picks per metre. Which uses more yarn per m² in total?
options: It cannot be found without counts
questions.explain: Plain: (2,400 + 2,000) × 1.209 = 5,320 m; rib: 2,400 × 1.57 + 2,000 × 1.00 = 5,768 m. The rib's heavy warp crimp outweighs its straight weft, so it uses more.

questions.q: Using 2,400 ends per m at 20.9 % crimp and 2,000 picks per m at 20.9 % crimp, what total yarn length in metres is needed per m² of jammed plain cloth? Give to the nearest metre.
A warp rib has 2,400 ends per m at 57 % crimp and 2,000 picks per m with no crimp. What total yarn length in metres is needed per m² of cloth?
questions.explain: 2,400 × 1.57 = 3,768 m of warp plus 2,000 m of weft = 5,768 m.

questions.q: Equal yarns are to be woven as densely as possible. Comparing plain weave and 2/2 twill with the lecture's crimp figures, which can be set denser and why?
options: 2/2 twill, because its lower crimp (13.1 %) means less bending between threads
Plain weave, because 1.732 d₁ is the smallest spacing any weave allows
Plain weave, because it has more interlacings to hold the threads
Both the same, since the yarn diameter is equal
questions.explain: The lecture ties crimp to how densely a cloth can be set; the twill's fewer interlacings and lower crimp let its threads lie closer. 1.732 d₁ is the plain-weave limit only.

questions.q: If the weft diameter is twice the warp diameter, the jammed spacing p₂ in the lecture (2.828 d₁) is larger than for equal yarns (1.732 d₁) because the warp must bend round a fatter weft.
questions.explain: A larger crossing yarn needs a longer path, so the minimum spacing grows from 1.732 d₁ to 2.828 d₁.

questions.q: A weaver's beam carries 3,200 ends, each 1,200 m long. With 8 % warp crimp, how many metres of cloth can be woven from it? Give to the nearest metre.
questions.explain: Cloth length = yarn length ÷ (1 + crimp) = 1,200 ÷ 1.08 = 1,111 m; the number of ends does not change the length.

questions.q: A student claims a 2/2 twill with 13.1 % crimp will be thinner than a jammed plain weave of the same yarns. Is that consistent with the lecture?
options: No: crimp has no effect on thickness
Yes, but only if the weft is two-fold
Yes: lower crimp means less bending out of the cloth plane, so a thinner, denser cloth
questions.explain: The lecture says crimp decides thickness; the twill's lower crimp means the yarns lie flatter.

questions.q: Which pair of statements is entirely correct?
options: Crimp is dimensionless; yarn length = cloth length × (1 + crimp)
Crimp is measured in cm; yarn length = cloth length ÷ (1 + crimp)
Crimp is a percentage of yarn length; cloth length = yarn length × (1 + crimp)
Crimp is dimensionless; yarn length = cloth length − crimp
questions.explain: Crimp is a ratio of lengths, and the yarn is longer than the cloth by the factor (1 + crimp); the other options invert or misplace the relation.
